Derived categoriesby Jean-Louis Verdier
1 Triangulated categories: definitions and examples
1.1 Definition of triangulated categories
Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an additive category, \(T\) an additive automorphism of \(\mathscr{A}\). Given two objects \(X\) and \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), we shall set
\[ \hom^i(X,Y) = \hom_\mathscr{A}(X,T^i(Y)) \qquad i\in \mathbb{Z} \]

Let \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) be three objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(\alpha\in \hom^i(X,Y)\), \(\beta\in \hom^j(X,Y)\). We shall define the composite \(\beta\circ\alpha\) belonging to \(\hom^{i+j}(X,Z)\) by:
\[ \beta\circ \alpha = \beta\circ T^i(\alpha) \text{.} \]

One checks that one thereby obtains a new category whose groups of morphisms between objects are graded. This new category will be called, by abuse of language: the category \(\mathscr{A}\), graded by the translation functor \(T\).
Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a category graded by a translation functor \(T\). Whenever one names or denotes a morphism without specifying the degree, it will always be a morphism of degree zero.

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{A}'\) be two additive categories graded by the functors \(T\) and \(T'\), \(F\) an additive functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to \(\mathscr{A}'\). One says that \(F\) is graded if one is given an isomorphism of functors1
\[ F\circ T = T'\circ F \]
The definition of the morphisms of graded functors is given in 4.1.1.

\(\mathscr{A}\) being an additive category graded by the functor \(T\), one calls a triangle a set of three objects \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) and of three morphisms \(u:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\), \(v:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z\), \(w:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} T(X)\) (\(\deg w=1\)). To designate the triangles one will use the notation \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) or else the diagram:
\[ \xymatrix{ & Z \ar[dl]_-w \\ X \ar[rr]^-u & & Y \ar[lu]_-v }\qquad \deg(w)=1 \]

Let \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\), \((X',Y',Z',u',v',w')\) be two triangles of \(\mathscr{A}\); a morphism from the first triangle to the second is a set of three morphisms \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X'\), \(g:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y'\), \(h:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z'\), such that the following diagram is commutative:
\[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-u \ar[d]^-f & Y \ar[r]^-v \ar[d]^-g & Z \ar[r]^-w \ar[d]^-h & T(X) \ar[d]^-{T(f)} \\ X' \ar[r]^-{u'} & Y' \ar[r]^-{v'} & Z' \ar[r]^-{w'} & T(X') } \]

One calls a triangulated category an additive category graded by a translation functor, equipped with a family of triangles that one calls the family of distinguished triangles. This family must moreover satisfy the axioms:
TR1
VIII:TR1

Every triangle isomorphic to a distinguished triangle is distinguished. Every morphism \(u:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) is contained in a distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\). The triangle \((X,X,0,\operatorname{id}_{X'},0,0)\) is distinguished.
TR2
VIII:TR2
For \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) to be distinguished, it is necessary and sufficient that \((Y,Z,T(X),v,w,-T(u))\) be distinguished.
TR3
VIII:TR3

\((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\), \((X',Y',Z',u',v',w')\) being distinguished, for every morphism \((f,g):u\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} u'\), there exists a morphism \(h:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z'\) such that \((f,g,h)\) is a morphism of triangles.
TR4
VIII:TR4

\[ \xymatrix{ & Z' \ar[dl]|{\deg=1} \\ X \ar[rr]^-u & & Y \ar[ul]_-i }\quad \xymatrix{ & X' \ar[dl]|{\deg(j)=1} \\ Y \ar[rr]^-v & & Z \ar[ul] }\quad \xymatrix{ & Y' \ar[dl]|{\deg=1} \\ X \ar[rr]^-w & & Z \ar[ul] } \]

being three distinguished triangles such that \(w=v\circ u\), there exist two morphisms \(f:Z'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y'\), \(g:Y' \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X'\) such that

1. \((\operatorname{id}_X, v, f)\) is a morphism of triangles

  2. \((u,\operatorname{id}_Z,g)\) is a morphism of triangles

  3. \((Z',Y',X',f,g,T(i) j)\) is a distinguished triangle

\(\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}'\) being two triangulated categories, one calls an exact functor from \(\mathscr{C}\) to \(\mathscr{C}'\) any additive, graded functor carrying distinguished triangles to distinguished triangles. The morphisms of exact functors are the morphisms of graded functors.
From the axioms VIII:TR1TR1, VIII:TR2TR2, VIII:TR3TR3 one immediately deduces the following property:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.1.2

Let \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) be a distinguished triangle and \(M\) an object of a triangulated category. One then has the exact sequences:

\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \hom^i(M,X) \ar[r]^-{\hom(M,u)} & \hom^i(M,Y) \ar[r]^-{\hom(M,v)} & \hom^i(M,Z) \ar[r]^-{\hom(M,w)} & \hom^{i+1}(M,X) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]
\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & \hom^i(Z,M) \ar[r]^-{\hom(v,M)} & \hom^i(Y,M) \ar[r]^-{\hom(u,M)} & \hom^i(X,M) \ar[r]^-{\hom(w,M)} & \hom^{i+1}(Z,M) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]
From this proposition one then deduces statements of the type:

• \((f,g,h)\) being a morphism of distinguished triangles and \(f,g\) isomorphisms.

  • The distinguished triangles built on a morphism (VIII:TR1TR1) are all isomorphic (but the isomorphisms are not, in general, uniquely determined).

  • When, in a distinguished triangle, one of the morphisms admits a kernel or a cokernel, the latter splits, i.e. it is of the form:

    \[ \xymatrix{ & Z+T(X) \ar[dl] \\ X+Y \ar[rr] & & Y+Z \ar[ul] } \]

  • The sum of two distinguished triangles is distinguished. (One uses the axiom VIII:TR4TR4.)
1.2 Examples
We shall first fix some notation. Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an additive category; \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) will denote the following category:

• The objects of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) will be the complexes of \(\mathscr{A}\), without restriction on the degree, with differential of degree \(+1\).

  • The morphisms of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) will be the morphisms of complexes (which commute with the differential) preserving the degree.
Let \(T\) be the following functor: for every object \(X^\bullet\) of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\)
\begin{align*} T(X^\bullet)_i &= (X^\bullet)_{i+1} \\ d_i(T(X^\bullet)) &= -d_{i+1}(X^\bullet) \text{.} \end{align*}

On morphisms the functor \(T\) acts in the following way: for every morphism \(f:X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet\), the morphism \(T(f):T(X^\bullet) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} T(Y^\bullet)\) is defined by
\[ T(f)_i = f_{i+1} \text{.} \]

One checks immediately that \(T\) is an additive automorphism of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). The morphisms of degree \(n\), defined by means of this translation functor, are then the morphisms that raise the degree by \(n\) and that commute or anticommute with the differential according to the parity of \(n\). One thus recovers the generally adopted definition.
\(\mathscr{C}\) will denote the following family of triangles: a triangle \((X^\bullet,Y^\bullet,Z^\bullet,u,v,w)\) is an element of the family if2

• \(Z^\bullet\) is the simple complex associated with the double complex

    \[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X^\bullet \ar[r]^-u & Y^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

    where the objects of \(Y^\bullet\) are the objects of first degree zero, and the objects of \(X^\bullet\) the objects of first degree \(-1\).

  • \(v\) is the image, under the functor: double complex \(\mapsto\) simple complex, of the morphism of double complexes:

    \[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0^\bullet \ar[r] \ar[d] & Y^\bullet \ar[r] \ar[d] & 0 \ar[r] \ar[d] & \cdots \\ \cdots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X^\bullet \ar[r] & Y^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

  • \(w\) is the opposite of the image, under the same functor, of the morphism of double complexes:

    \[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & \cdots \\ \cdots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] \ar[u] & X^\bullet \ar[r] \ar[u] & Y^\bullet \ar[r] \ar[u] & 0 \ar[r] \ar[u] & \cdots } \]

The set of morphisms homotopic to zero is a two-sided ideal (if \(f\) and \(g\) are composable and if \(f\) or \(g\) is homotopic to zero, the composite is homotopic to zero. If \(f\) and \(g\) are homotopic to zero, the morphism \(f\oplus g\) is homotopic to zero). For every pair of objects \(X^\bullet\), \(Y^\bullet\) one denotes by \(\operatorname{Htp}(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\) the subgroup of \(\hom_{\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\) consisting of the morphisms homotopic to zero. \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) will then be the category whose objects are the objects of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) and whose morphisms with source \(X^\bullet\) and target \(Y^\bullet\) are the group:
\[ \hom_{\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) / \operatorname{Htp}(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \text{.} \]

The composition law on the morphisms of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) is defined from the composition law on the morphisms of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) by passing to the quotient. \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) is an additive category. The translation functor \(T\) on \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) passes to the quotient (the translate of a morphism homotopic to zero is homotopic to zero). The functor obtained is an additive automorphism of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\), which we shall again denote by \(T\). By abuse of notation \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) will henceforth denote the category \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) graded by the functor \(T\).

One will call a distinguished triangle in \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) any triangle isomorphic to a triangle coming from \(\mathscr{C}\). The family of distinguished triangles satisfies the axioms VIII:TR1TR1, VIII:TR2TR2, VIII:TR3TR3 and VIII:TR4TR4. By abuse of notation \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) will denote the category \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) triangulated by the family of triangles defined above.
One moreover defines a whole arsenal of subcategories:

• A complex is said to be bounded below if all its objects of negative degree, save at most a finite number, are zero. One defines similarly the complexes bounded above, the bounded complexes. One will denote by \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^-(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^b(\mathscr{A})\) the full subcategories of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) generated by these families of objects. These subcategories are “triangulated subcategories” of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\): every distinguished triangle two of whose objects are objects of the subcategory is isomorphic to a triangle all three of whose objects are objects of the subcategory.

  • Suppose that \(\mathscr{A}\) is an abelian category. A complex is said to be cohomologically bounded below if all its cohomology objects of negative degree are zero except for a finite number of them. One defines analogously the cohomologically bounded above complexes, the cohomologically bounded complexes, the acyclic complexes. \(\mathsf{K}^{\infty,+}(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^{\infty,-}(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^{\infty,b}(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^{\infty,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A})\) will denote the full subcategories generated by these families of objects. These are triangulated subcategories.

    One will also have triangulated subcategories \(\mathsf{K}^{+,b}(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^{+,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A})\), …etc …(the first sign in the exponent gives information about the objects of the complexes, the second sign about the cohomology objects).

  • \(\mathscr{A}\) being no longer necessarily abelian, let \(O\) be a set of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\) stable under isomorphism and under direct sum. \(O(\mathscr{A})\) will denote the full subcategory of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) generated by the complexes whose objects in every degree are objects of \(O\). One will denote by \(\underline O(\mathscr{A})\) the corresponding triangulated subcategory in \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). When \(\mathscr{A}\) is abelian, one may take for the set \(O\) the set \(I\) of injectives or the set \(P\) of projectives.

\(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) is uniquely determined by the data of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) and of the family \(\mathscr{C}\). More precisely: every additive graded functor from \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) to a triangulated category that carries every triangle of \(\mathscr{C}\) to a distinguished triangle factors uniquely through \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\), and the functor obtained is exact.

For every complex \(X^\bullet\) of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\), \(\overline{X}^\bullet\) will denote the complex obtained from \(X^\bullet\) by setting the differential equal to zero. A three-term sequence:
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & X^\bullet \ar[r] & Y^\bullet \ar[r] & Z^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 } \]
will be called a semi-split sequence if the sequence
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \overline{X}^\bullet \ar[r] & \overline{Y}^\bullet \ar[r] & \overline{Z}^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 } \]
is split; i.e. if it is isomorphic to the sequence:
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & \overline{X}^\bullet \ar[r] & \overline{X}^\bullet + \overline{Z}^\bullet \ar[r] & \overline{Z}^\bullet \ar[r] & 0 . } \]

Let \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) be a semi-split sequence. Let us choose a splitting, i.e. for every \(n\) an isomorphism
\[ (Y^\bullet)^n \simeq (X^\bullet)^n + (Z^\bullet)^n \text{.} \]
The matrix of the differential of \(Y^\bullet\), in the direct-sum decomposition above, is of the form:
\[ \begin{pmatrix} d_{X^\bullet} & \varphi_n \\ 0 & d_{Y^\bullet} \end{pmatrix} \]
where \(\varphi_n\) is a morphism from \((Z^\bullet)^n\) to \((X^\bullet)^{n+1}\). The \(\varphi_n\) determine a morphism of complexes
\[ \varphi:Z^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} T(X^\bullet) \text{.} \]

When one changes the splitting, the class modulo homotopy of \(\varphi\) does not change. Moreover, denoting by \(\underline u\), \(\underline v\), \(\underline{\varphi}\) the images in \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) of the morphisms \(u\), \(v\), \(\varphi\), the triangle \((X^\bullet,Y^\bullet,Z^\bullet,\underline u,\underline v,\underline{\varphi})\) is distinguished. Let us denote by \(\mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A})\) the category of semi-split sequences of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\), and by \(\mathsf{TrK}(\mathscr{A})\) the category of distinguished triangles of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). The foregoing allows one to define a functor:
\[ \rho:\mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{TrK}(\mathscr{A}) \text{.} \]
This functor is essentially surjective.
1.3 Examples of cohomological functors and of exact functors

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) an abelian category. An additive functor \(F:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) is called a cohomological functor if for every distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\) the sequence

\[ \xymatrix{ F(X) \ar[r]^-{F(u)} & F(Y) \ar[r]^-{F(v)} & F(Z) } \]

is exact.
The functor \(F\circ T^i\) will often be denoted \(F^i\). By virtue of the axiom VIII:TR2TR2 of triangulated categories, one has the unbounded exact sequence:
\[ \xymatrix{ \cdots \ar[r] & F^i(X) \ar[r] & F^i(Y) \ar[r] & F^i(Z) \ar[r] & F^{i+-}(X) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]
1.3.2 Examples

1. Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category. For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\) the functor \(\hom_\mathscr{A}(X,-)\) is a cohomological functor. The functor \(\hom_\mathscr{A}(-,X)\) is a cohomological functor \(\mathscr{A}^\circ\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{Ab}\).

  2. Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an abelian category, \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) the category of complexes of \(\mathscr{A}\). One denotes by \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0:\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathscr{A}\) the following functor: Let \(X^\bullet\) be an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). One sets

    \[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0(X^\bullet) = \ker d^0 / \operatorname{im}{d^{-1}} \text{.} \]

    \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\) annihilates the morphisms homotopic to zero, hence factors uniquely through \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). One will again denote by \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0:\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}\) the functor obtained.
1.3.3 Example of an exact bifunctor
Let \(\mathscr{A}\), \(\mathscr{A}'\), \(\mathscr{A}''\) be three additive categories,
\[ P:\mathscr{A}\times \mathscr{A}'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}'' \]
a bilinear functor (i.e. additive with respect to each of the arguments separately). One then deduces from it the bilinear functor:
\[ P^\ast:\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\times \mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}') \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}'') \]
in the following way:

Let \(X^\bullet\) be an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) and \(Y^\bullet\) an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}')\). \(P(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\) is a double complex of \(\mathscr{A}''\). One then sets: \(P^\ast(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) = \) simple complex associated with \(P(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\).

Let \(f\) be a morphism of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}')\)) homotopic to zero and \(Z^\bullet\) an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}')\) (resp. \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\)). The morphism \(P^\ast(f,Z^\bullet)\) (resp. \(P^\bullet(Z^\bullet,f)\)) is then homotopic to zero. One deduces from this that \(P^\ast\) defines in a unique way a functor:
\[ P^\bullet:\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) \times \mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}') \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}'') \text{.} \]
\(P^\bullet\) is an exact bifunctor.
In particular, let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an additive category. One may take for \(P\) the functor:
\begin{align*} \mathscr{A}^\circ\times \mathscr{A} &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Ab} \\ (X,Y) &\mapsto \hom(X,Y) \end{align*}
One then obtains by the preceding construction a functor
\[ \hom^\bullet:\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})^\circ \times \mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}(\mathsf{Ab}) \]

which, composed with the functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0:\mathsf{K}(\mathsf{Ab})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Ab}\), evidently gives back the functor \(\hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}\).

blocks.html: 2 The quotient categories
2.1 Thick subcategories. Multiplicative systems of morphisms
We shall begin by giving two definitions.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1.1

A subcategory \(\mathscr{B}\) of a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}\) is said to be thick if \(\mathscr{B}\) is a full triangulated subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\) and if moreover \(\mathscr{B}\) has the following property:

For every morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) that factors through an object of \(\mathscr{B}\) and is contained in a distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,f,g,h)\), where \(Z\) is an object of \(\mathscr{B}\), the source of \(f\) and the target of \(f\) are objects of \(\mathscr{B}\).
The set of thick subcategories of \(\mathscr{A}\) will be denoted \(\mathscr{N}\).
The intersection of any family of thick subcategories is a thick subcategory.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category. A set \(S\) of morphisms of \(\mathscr{A}\) is called a multiplicative system of morphisms if it has the following five properties:

FR1

VIII:FR1 If \(f,g\in S\) and if \(f\) and \(g\) are composable, \(f\circ g\in S\). For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), the identity morphism of \(X\) is an element of \(S\).

FR2

VIII:FR2 In the category \(\mathscr{A}\), every diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ & Y \ar[d]^-{s\in S} \\ Z \ar[r]^-f & X } \]

can be completed into a commutative diagram

\[ \xymatrix{ P \ar[r]^-g \ar[d]^-{t\in S} & Y \ar[d]^-{s\in S} \\ Z \ar[r]^-f & X } \]

Moreover the symmetric property holds.

FR3

VIII:FR3 If \(f\) and \(g\) are morphisms, the following properties are equivalent:

  1. there exists an \(s\in S\) such that \(s\circ f=s\circ g\)

  2. there exists a \(t\in S\) such that \(f\circ t=g\circ t\)

FR4

VIII:FR4 Let \(T\) be the translation functor of \(\mathscr{A}\). For every element \(s\) of \(S\), \(T(s)\in S\).

FR5

VIII:FR5 \((X,Y,Z,u,v,w)\), \((X',Y',Z',u',v',w')\) being two distinguished triangles, \(f\) and \(g\) two elements of \(S\) such that the pair \((f,g)\) is a morphism from \(u\) to \(u'\), there exists a morphism \(h\in S\) such that \((f,g,h)\) is a morphism of triangles.
A multiplicative system of morphisms is said to be saturated if it has the following property:
A morphism \(f\) belongs to \(S\) if and only if there exist two morphisms \(g\) and \(g'\) such that \(g\circ f\in S\) and \(f\circ g'\in S\).
The intersection of any family of saturated multiplicative systems is a saturated multiplicative system.
The set of saturated multiplicative systems will be denoted \(\mathscr{S}\).

Let \(\mathscr{B}\) be a thick subcategory; one denotes by \(\varphi(\mathscr{B})\) the set of morphisms \(f\) that are contained in a distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,f,g,h)\) where \(Z\) is an object of \(\mathscr{B}\). \(\varphi(\mathscr{B})\) is a saturated multiplicative system.

Let \(S\) be a saturated multiplicative system; one denotes by \(\psi(S)\) the full subcategory generated by the objects \(Z\) contained in a distinguished triangle \((X,Y,Z,f,g,h)\) where \(f\) is an element of \(S\). The subcategory \(\psi(S)\) is a thick subcategory.

The main result of this section is then the following: \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism (preserving the order relation defined by inclusion) from \(\mathscr{N}\) onto \(\mathscr{S}\). The inverse isomorphism is none other than \(\psi\).
2.2 Universal problems

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{A}'\) be two triangulated categories and \(F\) an exact functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to \(\mathscr{A}'\). Let \(S(F)\) be the set of morphisms of \(\mathscr{A}\) that are carried by \(F\) to isomorphisms and \(\mathscr{B}(F)\) the full subcategory generated by the objects of \(\mathscr{A}\) that are carried by \(F\) to zero objects of \(\mathscr{A}'\). \(S(F)\) is a saturated multiplicative system and \(\mathscr{B}(F)\) is a thick subcategory. Moreover \(S(F) = \varphi(\mathscr{B}(F))\). Let then \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) a thick subcategory and \(S=\varphi(\mathscr{B})\) the corresponding saturated multiplicative system. The two universal problems below are equivalent.
Problem 1

VIII:prob1 To find a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\) and an exact functor \(Q:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\) such that every exact functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}'\) that carries the objects of \(\mathscr{B}\) to zero objects of \(\mathscr{A}'\) admits, in a unique way, a factorization of the form \(G\circ Q\) where \(G\) is an exact functor.
Problem 2

VIII:prob2 To find a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}_S\) and an exact functor \(Q:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}_S\) such that every exact functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}'\) that carries the morphisms of \(S\) to isomorphisms of \(\mathscr{A}'\) admits, in a unique way, a factorization of the form \(G\circ Q\) where \(G\) is an exact functor.

(The writer begs the reader's indulgence for the use of this outdated and old-fashioned language.) We shall show, in the following section, that VIII:prob2problem 2 admits a solution. Hence the corresponding VIII:prob1problem 1 admits the same solution.
2.3 Calculus of fractions

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(S\) a saturated multiplicative system. Let us denote by \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) the category of fractions of \(\mathscr{A}\) for the set of morphisms \(S\), and by \(Q\) the canonical functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\). The pair \((\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}],Q)\) solves the following problem: Every functor from \(\mathscr{A}\) to an arbitrary category (not necessarily additive) that carries the morphisms of \(S\) to isomorphisms factors, in a unique way, through \((\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}],Q)\). Such a pair always exists, with no hypothesis on the set of morphisms \(S\) [18]1. However the set of morphisms \(S\), being a saturated multiplicative system, has the properties VIII:FR1FR1, VIII:FR2FR2, VIII:FR3FR3. Consequently, by [18], the category \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) can be obtained by a calculus of fractions, on the right or on the left. We shall recall how one obtains \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) by a calculus of fractions on the right. (The calculus of fractions on the left is obtained by the procedure of reversing the arrows.)
The objects of \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) are the objects of \(\mathscr{A}\).

• For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), let \(S_X\) denote the category of arrows belonging to \(S\), having target \(X\). To every object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{A}\) one associates, functorially in \(Y\), the following functor on \(S_X^\circ\) with values in the category of sets: (\(S_X^\circ\) denotes the opposite category)

    \[ H_Y:s\mapsto \hom(\operatorname{source}(s),Y) \text{.} \]

    One then sets:

    \[ \hom_{\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]}(X,Y) = \varinjlim_{S_X^\circ} H_Y \text{.} \]

    For everything concerning inductive limits, we refer to [1].

    One then observes, with pleasure, using VIII:FR1FR1, VIII:FR2FR2, VIII:FR3FR3, that the category \(S_X^\circ\) possesses the properties L1, L2, L3. The inductive limits therefore possess all the good properties of inductive limits over filtered ordered sets.

  • Let \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) be three objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(a\) an element of \(\hom_{\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]}(X,Y)\) and \(b\) an element of \(\hom_{\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]}(Y,Z)\). Let \(s\) be an object of \(S_X\), \(\underline a\) an element of \(\hom(\operatorname{source}(s),Y)\) whose image is \(a\), and an object of \(S_y\), \(\underline b\) an element of \(\hom(\operatorname{source}(t),Z)\) whose image is \(b\). One then has a diagram:

    \[ \tag{1} \xymatrix{ & \bullet \ar[dl]_-s \ar[dr]^-{\underline a} & & \bullet \ar[dl]_-t \ar[dr]^-{\underline b} \\ X & & Y & & Z } \]

    which, by VIII:FR2FR2, can be completed into a diagram:

    \[ \xymatrix{ & & \bullet \ar[dl]_-{t'} \ar[dr]^-{\underline c} \\ & \bullet \ar[dl]_-s \ar[dr]^-{\underline a} & & \bullet \ar[dl]_-t \ar[dr]^-{\underline b} \\ X & & Y & & Z } \]

    Let us denote by \(b\circ a\) the image in \(\hom_{\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]}(X,Z)\) of the morphism \(\underline{b\circ c}\). One checks that, thanks to the properties VIII:FR1FR1, VIII:FR2FR2, VIII:FR3FR3, \(b\circ a\) does not depend on the chosen representatives \(\underline a\) and \(\underline b\), and that it also does not depend on the manner of completing the diagram (1). One checks moreover that one has thereby defined a category \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\).
We shall denote by \(Q\) the obvious functor: \(\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\).

Since \(\mathscr{A}\) is an additive category, \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) is an additive category. Moreover, using VIII:FR4FR4 one shows that there exists one and only one translation functor on \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\), which we shall denote by \(T\), satisfying the relation:
\[ Q\circ T = T\circ Q \text{.} \]

Finally, with the help of VIII:FR5FR5, one shows that there exists one and only one triangulated structure on \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) such that the functor \(Q\) is exact. The distinguished triangles of \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) are none other than the triangles isomorphic to the images, under \(Q\), of the distinguished triangles of \(\mathscr{A}\). Denoting by \(\mathscr{A}_S\) the category \(\mathscr{A}[S^{-1}]\) equipped with this triangulated structure, one shows without difficulty that the pair \((\mathscr{A}_S,Q)\) is a solution to VIII:prob2problem 2.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.3.3

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\), \((Q,\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B})\) the solution of VIII:prob1problem 1 (§2.2). \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\) will be called the quotient category of \(\mathscr{A}\) by \(\mathscr{B}\). \(Q\) will be called the canonical passage-to-the-quotient functor. More generally, let \(\mathscr{N}\) be a triangulated subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\) and let \(\underline{\mathscr{N}}\) be the smallest thick subcategory containing \(\mathscr{N}\). The quotient category of \(\mathscr{A}\) by \(\mathscr{N}\): \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}\) will by definition be \(\mathscr{A}/\underline{\mathscr{N}}\).
2.4 Properties of quotient categories

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category and \(H\) a cohomological functor with values in an abelian category \(\mathscr{G}\). Let \(\mathscr{B}_H\) be the full subcategory generated by the objects all of whose translates are transformed by \(H\) into zero objects of \(\mathscr{G}\), and \(S_H\) the set of morphisms all of whose translates are transformed by \(H\) into isomorphisms of \(\mathscr{G}\). \(\mathscr{B}_H\) is a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\); \(S_H\) is a saturated multiplicative system. Moreover \(S_H=\varphi(\mathscr{B}_H)\) (§2.1). The functor \(H\) factors in a unique manner through \((Q,\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}_H)\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.4.2

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) a triangulated subcategory, \(\mathscr{N}\) a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(S=\varphi(\mathscr{N})\) the corresponding saturated multiplicative system.

  1. The category \(\mathscr{N}\cap\mathscr{B}\) is a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{B}\). The corresponding multiplicative system is \(S\cap \mathscr{B}\).

  2. The two following properties are equivalent:

    1. For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{B}\) and every morphism \(s:R\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\) where \(s\) is an element of \(S\), there exists a morphism \(s':R'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} R\) where \(s\circ'\) is an element of \(S\cap \mathscr{B}\); and \(R'\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathscr{B}\).

    2. Every morphism from an object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{B}\) into an object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{N}\) factors through an object of \(\mathscr{N}\cap \mathscr{B}\).

  3. The properties (i)' and (ii)' obtained from (i) and (ii) by reversing the arrows are equivalent.

  4. If properties (i) and (ii) hold, or else if properties (i)' and (ii)' hold, the canonical functor

    \[ \xymatrix{ \mathscr{B}/\mathscr{N}\cap \mathscr{B} \ar[r] & \mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N} } \]

    is faithful.

    Since this functor is injective on objects, it realizes \(\mathscr{B}/\mathscr{N}\cap\mathscr{B}\) as a subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}\).

  5. If moreover \(\mathscr{B}\) is a full subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(\mathscr{B}/\mathscr{N}\cap \mathscr{B}\) is a full subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{N}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4.3

Let \(\mathscr{A}\subset \mathscr{B}\subset \mathscr{C}\) be three triangulated categories, \(\mathscr{A}\) a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{B}\), \(\mathscr{B}\) a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{C}\). Then \(\mathscr{A}\) is a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{C}\), \(\mathscr{B}/\mathscr{A}\) is a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{A}\). The canonical functor \(\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{B} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} (\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{A})/(\mathscr{B}/\mathscr{A})\) is an isomorphism.
2.5 Properties of the passage-to-the-quotient functor

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) a thick subcategory, \(S\) the corresponding multiplicative system, \(Q:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\) the canonical passage-to-the-quotient functor.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5.1

\(X\) and \(Y\) being objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), the following assertions are equivalent:

  1. Every morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) such that there exists a morphism \(s:Z\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\), in \(S\), satisfying \(f\circ s=0\), is a zero morphism.

  2. Every morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) such that there exists a morphism \(s:Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z\), \(s\in S\), satisfying \(s\circ f=0\), is a zero morphism.

  3. Every morphism \(f:X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) that factors through an object of \(\mathscr{B}\) is zero.

  4. The canonical map:

    \[ \hom_\mathscr{A}(X,Y) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \hom_{\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}}(Q(X),Q(Y)) \]

    is injective.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5.2

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two objects of \(\mathscr{A}\). The following assertions are equivalent:

  1. Every diagram (\(s\in S\)):

    \[ \xymatrix{ & Z \ar[dl]_-s \ar[dr]^-f \\ X & & Y } \]

    is completed into a diagram: \((s,t\in S\)):

    \[ \xymatrix{ & Z' \ar[d]_-t \\ & Z \ar[dl]_-s \ar[dr]^-f \\ X & & Y } \]

    where \(f\circ t\) factors through \((X,s\circ t)\).

  2. Assertion obtained by reversing the direction of the arrows in (a) and interchanging \(X\) and \(Y\).

  3. Every diagram:

    \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[r]^-f & N \ar[r]^-g & Y } \]

    where \(g\circ f=0\) and where \(N\) is an object of \(\mathscr{B}\), is completed into a diagram:

    \[ \xymatrix{ & N' \ar[d]^-i \\ X \ar[ur]^-h \ar[r]^-f & N \ar[r]^-g & Y } \]

    where \(f=i\circ h\) and where \(g\circ i=0\).

  4. Assertion obtained by changing the direction of the arrows in (c) and interchanging \(X\) and \(Y\).

  5. The canonical map:

    \[ \xymatrix{ \hom_{\mathscr{A}}(X,Y) \ar[r]^-Q & \hom_{\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}}(Q(X),Q(Y)) } \]

    is surjective.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.5.3

Let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathscr{A}\). The following assertions are equivalent:

  1. For every object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), the canonical map

    \[ \xymatrix{ \hom_{\mathscr{A}}(X,Y) \ar[r]^-Q & \hom_{\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}}(Q(X),Q(Y)) } \]

    is an isomorphism.

  2. Every morphism from \(X\) into an object of \(\mathscr{B}\) is zero.

Similarly, the two following assertions are equivalent:

  1. For every object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), the canonical map:

    \[ \xymatrix{ \hom_{\mathscr{A}}(X,Y) \ar[r]^-Q & \hom_{\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}}(Q(X),Q(Y)) } \]

    is an isomorphism.

  2. Every morphism from an object of \(\mathscr{B}\) into \(X\) is zero.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.5.4

Every object possessing the equivalent properties (a) and (b) of the preceding proposition will be called an object free on the left over \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\), or else again an object \(Q\)-free on the left. Similarly, every object possessing the equivalent properties (a)' and (b)' will be called an object free on the right over \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\), or again an object \(Q\)-free on the right. It is defined up to isomorphism by the knowledge of \(Q(X)\in\operatorname{Ob}{\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}}\).
2.6 Functors adjoint to the passage-to-the-quotient functor

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.6.1

Two triangulated subcategories \(\mathscr{N}\) and \(\mathscr{N}'\) of a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}\) are said to be orthogonal if for every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{N}\) and every object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{N}'\), one has:

\[ \hom_\mathscr{A}(X,Y) = 0 \]

\(\mathscr{N}'\) will then be said to be orthogonal on the right to \(\mathscr{N}\), and \(\mathscr{N}\) orthogonal on the left to \(\mathscr{N}'\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.2

Let \(\mathscr{N}\) be a triangulated subcategory of a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}\). The full category \(\mathscr{N}^\bot\) (resp. \(^\bot\mathscr{N}\)) generated by the objects \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\) such that for every object \(Y\) of \(\mathscr{N}\) one has \(\hom_\mathscr{A}(Y,X)=0\) (resp. \(\hom_\mathscr{A}(X,Y)=0\)), is a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\). The category \(\mathscr{N}^\bot\) is called, by abuse of language, the orthogonal on the right of \(\mathscr{N}\).
This proposition allows us to reformulate proposition 2.5.3.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.3

Let \(\mathscr{B}\subset\mathscr{A}\) be a thick subcategory of a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}\). The full category generated by the objects free on the right over \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\) (resp. on the left) is none other than the orthogonal on the right (resp. on the left) of \(\mathscr{B}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.4

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be a triangulated category, \(\mathscr{B}\) a thick subcategory of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(\mathscr{B}^\bot\) the orthogonal on the right of \(\mathscr{B}\), \(S(\mathscr{B})\), \(s(\mathscr{B}^\bot)\) the corresponding multiplicative systems, \(Q\) and \(Q^\bot\) the canonical passage-to-the-quotient functors. For an object \(x\) of \(\mathscr{A}\), let us consider the following properties:

  1. \(X\) maps by a morphism of \(S(\mathscr{B})\) into an object of \(\mathscr{B}^\bot\).

  2. \(X\) receives, by a morphism of \(S(\mathscr{B}^\bot)\), an object of \(\mathscr{B}\).

  3. The category \(S_X(\mathscr{B})\) of the arrows of \(S(\mathscr{B})\) with source \(X\) admits a final object.

  4. The category \(S^X(\mathscr{B}^\bot)\) of the arrows of \(S(\mathscr{B}^\bot)\) with target \(X\) admits an initial object.

  5. The category \(\mathscr{B}/X\) of the objects of \(\mathscr{B}\) over \(X\) admits a final object.

  6. The category \(\mathscr{B}^\bot/X\) of the objects of \(\mathscr{B}^\bot\) under \(X\) admits an initial object.

One then has

\[ \xymatrix@=0.5cm{ & & & & (iv) \\ (i) \ar@{<=>}[r] & (ii) \ar@{<=>}[r] & (iii) \ar@{<=>}[r] & (v) \ar@{=>}[ur] \ar@{=>}[dr] \\ & & & & (vi) } \]

If moreover \(^\bot(\mathscr{B}^\bot)=\mathscr{B}\), then all the properties are equivalent.

Let \(\mathscr{B}\) be a thick subcategory of a triangulated category \(\mathscr{A}\), \(i\) the injection functor of \(\mathscr{B}\) into \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(Q\) the passage-to-the-quotient functor of \(\mathscr{A}\) into \(\mathscr{A}/\mathscr{B}\), \(\mathscr{B}^\bot\) the orthogonal on the right of \(\mathscr{B}\), \(i^\bot\) and \(Q^\bot\) the corresponding functors. One deduces immediately from proposition 2.6.4 the following propositions:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.5

The two following properties are equivalent:

  1. The functor \(i\) admits a right adjoint.

  2. The functor \(Q\) admits a right adjoint.
The proposition is still true when one replaces the word right by the word left.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.6

The two following properties are equivalent:

  1. The functor \(i\) admits a right adjoint.

  2. The functor \(i^\bot\) admits a left adjoint. The orthogonal on the left of the category \(\mathscr{B}^\bot\) is equal to \(\mathscr{B}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6.7

Suppose the properties of propositions 2.6.5 and 2.6.6 are satisfied. Let \(i^\ast\) and \(Q^\ast\) be the right adjoints of \(i\) and \(Q\). Similarly, let \(^\ast i^\bot\) and \(^\ast Q^\bot\) be the left adjoints of \(i^\bot\) and of \(Q^\bot\). All these functors are exact. Moreover:

There exists a functorial isomorphism \(Q^\ast\circ Q\xrightarrow{\sim} i^\bot\circ ^\ast i^\bot\) such that the diagram below is commutative:

\[ \xymatrix{ & \operatorname{id} \ar[dl] \ar[dr] \\ Q^\ast \circ Q \ar[rr]^\sim & & i^\bot\circ ^\ast i^\bot } \]

(the oblique arrows are defined by the adjunction properties).

There exists, similarly, an isomorphism \(^\ast Q^\bot \circ Q^\bot \xrightarrow{\sim} i\circ i^\ast\) such that the following diagram is commutative:

\[ \xymatrix{ ^\ast Q^\bot\circ Q^\bot \ar[rr]^-\sim \ar[dr] & & i\circ i^\ast \ar[dl] \\ & \operatorname{id}{} } \]

Finally, there exists a functorial morphism of degree \(1\): \(\partial:i^\bot\circ ^\ast i^\bot \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} i\circ i^\ast\) such that the following triangle is distinguished \((\deg\partial=1\)):

\[ \xymatrix{ i^\bot \circ ^\ast i^\bot \ar[rr]^-\partial & & i\circ i^\ast \ar[dl] \\ & \operatorname{id}{} \ar[ul] } \]

Such a morphism \(\delta\) is unique and satisfies \(\delta(T X_0) = - T \delta(X)\) (\(X\) object \(q\circ q\), \(T\) translation).

footnotes.html: The original text references [C.G.G] here. Most likely, this is the lost work Catégories et foncteurs by Chevalley, Gabriel and Grothendieck, referenced in[31].

pages.title: The derived categories of an abelian category

blocks.html: 3 The derived categories of an abelian category
3.1 The derived categories
We use the notations of 1.2.3. We shall use in addition the following notations:
3.1.1 Notations
Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an abelian category. We set:

\begin{align*} \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{\infty,\infty}(\mathscr{A})/\mathsf{K}^{\infty,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{b,b}(\mathscr{A})/\mathsf{K}^{b,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{+,+}(\mathscr{A}) / \mathsf{K}^{+,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{-,-}(\mathscr{A}) / \mathsf{K}^{-,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \text{.} \end{align*}

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.2

The natural functors appearing in the following diagram:

\[ \xymatrix@=0.5cm{ & \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ur] & & \mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ul] \\ & \mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ul] \ar[ur] } \]

are fully faithful.

The natural functors:

\begin{align*} \mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{b,b}(\mathscr{A})/\mathsf{K}^{b,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}^{+,b}(\mathscr{A})/\mathsf{K}^{+,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A}) &= \mathsf{K}^{b,b}(\mathscr{A})/\mathsf{K}^{b,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}^{-,b}(\mathscr{A}) / \mathsf{K}^{-,\varnothing}(\mathscr{A}) \end{align*}

are equivalences of categories.

The functors of the diagram:

\[ \xymatrix@=0.5cm{ & \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) \\ \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ur] & & \mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ul] \\ & \mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A}) \ar[ul] \ar[ur] } \]

being injective on objects, realize the categories \(\mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A})\) as full subcategories of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\).
The proof of this proposition is found in theorem 2.4.2.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.3

The category \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) will be called the derived category of the category \(\mathscr{A}\). The objects of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) isomorphic to the objects of \(\mathsf{D}^b(\mathscr{A})\) will be called the bounded objects of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\). The objects of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) isomorphic to the objects of \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\) will be called the objects bounded on the left, the objects of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) isomorphic to the objects of \(\mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A})\) will be called the objects bounded on the right.
We shall denote by \(D\) the canonical functor:
\[ D : \mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) \text{.} \]

The “restriction” of \(D\) to the full subcategory \(\mathscr{A}\) of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) will again be denoted \(D\). The functor \(D\) restricted to \(\mathscr{A}\) is fully faithful. The functor \(D\) factors in a unique manner through \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two objects of \(\mathscr{A}\).
One checks without difficulty that for every \(m\geqslant 0\), the groups:
\[ \hom_{\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})}(D(X),T^{-m} D(Y)) \qquad \text{(} T \text{ is the translation functor)} \]
are zero. The cohomological dimension of \(\mathscr{A}\) will be the smallest of the integers \(n\) such that for every \(m>n\) one has:
\[ \hom_{\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})}(D(X),T^m D(Y)) = 0 \qquad\text{for every pair } X,Y \text{ of objects of } \mathscr{A} \text{.} \]
If there are no such integers, one says that the cohomological dimension of \(\mathscr{A}\) is infinite.

Let us denote by \(\mathsf{I}^+(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{I}(\mathscr{A})\)) the full triangulated subcategory of \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\)) defined by the complexes whose objects are injective in every degree.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.4

Suppose that the category \(\mathscr{A}\) has enough injectives. The natural functor:

\[ Q^+:\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) \]

induces an equivalence of categories:

\[ \mathsf{I}^+(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) \text{.} \]

The quasi-inverse functor is a right adjoint of \(Q^+\).
If moreover \(\mathscr{A}\) is of finite cohomological dimension, the preceding assertion remains true when one deletes the exponents \(+\) from it.
There is an analogous statement concerning the projectives.
The proof of proposition 3.1.4 rests on 2.6.4.
The triangulated structure of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) is made precise by the following proposition.

Let \(\mathsf{E}(\mathscr{A})\) be the category of three-term exact sequences of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). The category \(\mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A})\) of semi-split exact sequences (§1.2.4) is a full subcategory of \(\mathsf{E}(\mathscr{A})\). One has defined (loc. cit.) a functor:
\[ \rho:\mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{TrK}(\mathscr{A}) \]
where \(\mathsf{TrK}(\mathscr{A})\) denotes the category of distinguished triangles of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). From this one deduces a functor
\[ \sigma : \mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{TrD}(\mathscr{A}) \]
where \(\mathsf{TrD}(\mathscr{A})\) denotes the category of distinguished triangles of \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.5

There exists one and only one functor:

\[ \Pi:\mathsf{E}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{TrD}(\mathscr{A}) \]

of the form (\(\deg \delta(S)=1\)):

\[ (S=0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0) \mapsto \xymatrix{ & D(Z^\bullet) \ar[dl]_-{\delta(S)} \\ D(X^\bullet) \ar[rr]^-{D(u)} & & D(Y^\bullet) \ar[ul]_-{D(v)} } \]

whose restriction to \(\mathsf{SSS}(\mathscr{A})\) is \(\sigma\). This functor is essentially surjective.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.6

The canonical cohomological functor:

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0:\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A} \]

factors in a unique manner through a functor that we shall again denote \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0:\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A} \text{.} \]

On \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) the functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0\) and its translates \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i\) form a conservative system, i.e. a morphism \(f:X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet\) is an isomorphism if and only if for every integer \(i\)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(f):\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y) \]

is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.7

A morphism \(f:X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet\) of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\)) is called a quasi-isomorphism when for every integer \(i\)

\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(f):\underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(X) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \underline{\operatorname{H}}^i(Y) \]

is an isomorphism.
By the preceding proposition, the quasi-isomorphisms are the morphisms that become isomorphisms in \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.1.8

Let \(\sigma\) be a set of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), \(X^\bullet\) an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\)). A right (resp. left) resolution of type \(\sigma\) of \(X^\bullet\) is a quasi-isomorphism \(X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} V^\bullet\) (resp. \(V^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X^\bullet\)) where \(V^\bullet\) is a complex all of whose objects belong to \(\sigma\). One will say injective resolution (resp. projective) instead of right (resp. left) resolution of injective (resp. projective) type.
In general, one will allow oneself to omit the words “right” or “left” when no ambiguity results from it.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.9

  1. Suppose that every object of \(\mathscr{A}\) injects into an object of \(\sigma\) (resp. is a quotient of an object of \(\sigma\)). Then every object of \(\mathsf{C}^+(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. of \(\mathsf{C}^-(\mathscr{A})\)) admits a right resolution (resp. left) of type \(\sigma\) in \(\mathsf{C}^+(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. in \(\mathsf{C}^-(\mathscr{A})\)).

  2. Suppose moreover that there exists an integer \(n\) such that for every exact sequence:

    \begin{align*} Y^0 &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^{n-1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0 \\ \text{(resp. } 0 &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^n \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^{n-1} \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \cdots \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^1 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^0 \text{)} \end{align*}

    of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\) where, for every \(i\), \(0\leqslant i\leqslant n-1\), \(Y^i\) is an object of \(\sigma\), the object \(Y^n\) is an object of \(\sigma\). Then every object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) admits a right (resp. left) resolution of type \(\sigma\).
3.2 Study of the \(\operatorname{Ext}\)

Let \(X^\bullet\) and \(Y^\bullet\) be two objects of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\)) and \(D:\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(Q:\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\)) the functor canonical.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.2.1

One calls \(i\)-th hyper-ext and denotes:

\[ (X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\mapsto \operatorname{Ext}^i(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \]

the functor: \(\hom_{\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})}(D(X^\bullet),T^i D(Y^\bullet))\) (resp. \(\hom_{\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})}(Q(X^\bullet),T^i Q(Y^\bullet))\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.2

Let \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Z^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) be an exact sequence of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). Let \(V^\bullet\) be an object of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). One has the unbounded exact sequences:

\[ \xymatrix@=0.5cm{ \cdots \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(V^\bullet,X^\bullet) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(V^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(V^\bullet,Z^\bullet) \ar[r]^-\delta & \operatorname{Ext}^{i+1}(V^\bullet,X^\bullet) \ar[r] & \cdots \\ \cdots \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(Z^\bullet,V^\bullet) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(Y^\bullet,V^\bullet) \ar[r] & \operatorname{Ext}^i(X^\bullet,V^\bullet) \ar[r]^-\delta & \operatorname{Ext}^{i+1}(Z^\bullet,V^\bullet) \ar[r] & \cdots } \]

Let \(X^\bullet\) and \(Y^\bullet\) be two objects of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\). One denotes by \(\mathsf{Qis}/X^\bullet\) (resp. \(\mathsf{Qis}^+/X^\bullet\), \(\mathsf{Qis}^-/X^\bullet\), \(\mathsf{Qis}^b/X^\bullet\)) the category of quasi-isomorphisms with target \(X^\bullet\) and source in \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) (resp. \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^-(\mathscr{A})\), \(\mathsf{K}^b(\mathscr{A})\)). Similarly one defines the categories \(Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}\), \(Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}^+\),… (quasi-isomorphisms with source \(Y^\bullet)\).
We propose to summarize in the following proposition the various equivalent definitions of the \(\operatorname{Ext}^i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.3

1. There exist isomorphisms of functors:

\[ \xymatrix{ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) = \hom_{\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})}(Q(X^\bullet),Q(Y^\bullet)) \ar[r]^-\sim & \varinjlim_{(\mathsf{Qis}/X^\bullet)^\circ} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(-,Y^\bullet) \ar[r]^-\sim & \\ \varinjlim_{Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,-) \ar[r]^-\sim & \varinjlim_{(\mathsf{Qis}/X^\bullet)^\circ \times Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(-,-) . } \]

If \(X^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^-(\mathscr{A})\):

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \varinjlim_{(\mathsf{Qis}^-/X^\bullet)^\circ} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(-,Y^\bullet) \]

If \(Y^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\):

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \varinjlim_{Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,-) \]

If \(X^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^-(\mathscr{A})\) and if \(Y^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^b(\mathscr{A})\):

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \varinjlim_{Y^\bullet/\mathsf{Qis}^b} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,-) \]

If \(X^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^b(\mathscr{A})\) and \(Y^\bullet\) an object of \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\):

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \varinjlim_{(\mathsf{Qis}^b/X^\bullet)^\circ} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(-,Y^\bullet) \]

If the category \(\mathscr{A}\) has enough injectives and if \(Y^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\), then \(Y^\bullet\) admits one and only one injective resolution (up to isomorphism in \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\)):

\[ Y^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} I(Y^\bullet) \]

and we have:

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,I(Y^\bullet)) \text{.} \]

We likewise have an analogous statement for projectives. If the category \(\mathscr{A}\) admits enough injectives and if \(\mathscr{A}\) is of finite cohomological dimension, then every object \(Y^\bullet\) of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) admits one and only one injective resolution:

\[ Y^\bullet \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} I(Y^\bullet) \]

and we have:

\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \xrightarrow{\sim} \hom_{\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})}(X^\bullet,I(Y^\bullet)) \]

Analogous statement for projectives.
Remark:
By making the isomorphism of Proposition 3.2.3(3) explicit, we recover Yoneda's definition.
4 The derived functors
4.1 Definition of derived functors

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.1

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}'\) be two graded categories (we denote by \(T\) the translation functor of \(\mathscr{C}\) and of \(\mathscr{C}'\)), and \(F\) and \(G\) two graded functors from \(\mathscr{C}\) to \(\mathscr{C}'\). A morphism of graded functors is a morphism of functors:

\[ u:F\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} G \]

which has the following property:

For every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{C}\), the following diagram is commutative:

\[ \xymatrix{ F(T X) \ar[r]^-{u(T X)} & G(T X) \\ T F(X) \ar[r]^-{T u(X)} \ar[u]_-\wr & T G(X) \ar[u]_-\wr } \]

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}'\) be two triangulated categories. We denote by \(\mathsf{Fex}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{C}')\) the category of exact functors from \(\mathscr{C}\) to \(\mathscr{C}'\), the morphisms between two functors being the morphisms of graded functors.

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(\Phi:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})\) an exact functor (\(\ast\) and \(\ast'\) denote one of the signs \(+\), \(-\), \(b\), or \(v\) “empty”). The canonical functor \(Q:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\) gives us, by composition, a functor
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{Fex}(\mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})) \ar[r] & \mathsf{Fex}(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})) } \]

whence (also denoting by \(Q'\) the canonical functor \(\mathsf{K}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})\)) a functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)): \(\mathsf{Fex}(\mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Ab}\):
\begin{align*} \Psi &\mapsto \hom(Q'\circ \Phi,\Psi\circ Q) \\ (\text{resp. }\Psi &\mapsto \hom(\Psi\circ Q,Q'\circ \Phi)\text{ ).} \end{align*}

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.2

We shall say that \(\Phi\) admits a total derived functor on the right (resp. on the left) if the functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)) is representable. An object representing the functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)) will be called the total derived functor on the right (resp. on the left) of \(\Phi\) and will be denoted \(\mathsf{R} \Phi\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} \Phi\)).1
4.1.3 Notations

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) an additive functor. The total derived functor on the right of the functor \(\mathsf{K}^+(f):\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{B})\) will be denoted \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\). One defines similarly \(\mathsf{R}^- f\), \(\mathsf{R} f\), \(\mathsf{L}^+ f\), \(\mathsf{L}^- f\), \(\mathsf{L} f\).

Similarly, let \(F:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) be a cohomological functor. The canonical quotient functor \(Q:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\) defines, by composition, a functor:
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{Foco}(\mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathscr{B}) \ar[r] & \mathsf{Foco}(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathscr{B}) } \]

(\(\mathsf{Foco}(-,-)\) denotes the category of cohomological functors) whence a functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)) \(\mathsf{Foco}(\mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A}),\mathscr{B}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Ab}\), \(G\mapsto \hom(F,G\circ Q)\) (resp. \(G\mapsto \hom(G\circ Q,F)\)).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.4

We shall say that the functor \(F\) admits a cohomological derived functor on the right (resp. on the left) if the functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)) is representable. An object representing the functor \(\%\) (resp. \(\%'\)) will be called the cohomological derived functor on the right (resp. on the left) and will be denoted \(\mathsf{R} F\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} F\)).
4.1.5 Notations

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) an additive functor. The cohomological derived functor on the right of the functor:
\[ \underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}\circ \mathsf{K}^+ f:\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B} \]

will be denoted \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\). When no confusion results, the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\circ T^i\) (\(T\) is the translation functor) will be denoted \(\mathsf{R}^i f\). The cohomological derived functor on the right of the functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}{}\circ \mathsf{K} f\) will be denoted \(\mathsf{R} f\). When no confusion results, the functor \(\mathsf{R} f\circ T^i\) will be denoted \(\mathsf{R}^i f\).
One defines similarly the functors \(\mathsf{L}^- f\), \(\mathsf{L} f\), \(\mathsf{L}^i f\).
4.1.6 Remarks

These definitions contain, as we shall see in the following section, the classical definition of derived functors when the categories have enough injectives or projectives and the complexes are suitably bounded. They are, however, more general. But without further hypotheses they are not very tractable. For example, let \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) be an additive functor between two abelian categories. Suppose that the functors \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) and \(\mathsf{R} f\) exist. I do not know how to prove that \(\mathsf{R} f\) induces on \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\) the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\). Suppose moreover that the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) (cohomological derived functor) exists. I do not know how to prove that the functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}\circ \mathsf{R}^+ f\) is isomorphic to the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\). Nevertheless, in practice these properties will be satisfied.
4.2 Existence of derived functors

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.1

The hypotheses are those of Definition 4.1.4. Suppose in addition that \(\mathscr{A}\) is a \(\mathscr{U}\)-category, where \(\mathscr{U}\) is a universe such that the set \(\mathbb{Z}\) of rational integers is an element of \(\mathscr{U}\), and such that the set of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\) is an element of \(\mathscr{U}\). Suppose moreover that the category \(\mathscr{B}\) is the category of \(\mathscr{U}\)-abelian groups, or more generally the category of sheaves of \(\mathscr{U}\)-abelian groups on an arbitrary \(\mathscr{U}\)-site. (A \(\mathscr{U}\)-site is a \(\mathscr{U}\)-category whose set of objects is an element of \(\mathscr{U}\), equipped with a topology.) The functor \(F\) admits a cohomological derived functor on the right. This functor is computed in the following way:

Let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\), and \(\underline X\) the object of \(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\) above \(X\). We then have a functorial isomorphism:

\[ \mathsf{R} F(X) = \varinjlim_{\underline X/\mathsf{Qis}^\ast} F(-) \text{.} \]

In particular, let \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) be an additive functor. The functors \(\mathsf{R} f\) and \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) exist and are computed in the manner indicated above. The functor \(\mathsf{R} f\) induces on \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\) the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\). Since no confusion can then result, we shall use the notation \(\mathsf{R}^i f\).
4.2.2 Remarks

One can express Proposition 4.2.1 in a more general form within the framework of triangulated categories. The hypotheses to be made on the category \(\mathscr{B}\), in order to ensure the validity of Proposition 4.2.1, are hypotheses of existence and exactness of inductive limits along pseudo-filtered \(\mathscr{U}\)-categories whose sets of objects are elements of \(\mathscr{U}\). Proposition 4.2.1 introduces an asymmetry between the right derived functors and the left derived functors, at least in practice.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.2.3

The data are those of Definition 4.1.2. We are moreover given a full triangulated subcategory of \(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\): \(\mathscr{C}\), and we denote by \(\mathscr{N}\) the full triangulated subcategory of the objects of \(\mathscr{C}\) that are acyclic. Suppose that

  1. Every object of \(\mathscr{N}\) is transformed by \(\Phi\) into an acyclic object of \(\mathsf{K}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})\).

  2. Every object \(X\) of \(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\) is the source (resp. target) of a quasi-isomorphism whose target (resp. source) is an object of \(\mathscr{C}\).

  1. Then \(\Phi\) admits a total derived functor on the right (resp. on the left).

  2. The functor \(\mathsf{R} \Phi\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} \Phi\)) is obtained in the following manner:

    The restriction of the functor \(Q'\circ \Phi:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})\) to the category \(\mathscr{C}\) vanishes on the objects of \(\mathscr{N}\), hence factors through \(\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{N}\). One thus obtains a functor \(\Phi':\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{N}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^{\ast'}(\mathscr{B})\). But the natural functor \(\mathscr{C}/\mathscr{N}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\) is an equivalence of categories (Theorem 2.4.2). Whence, by composing with the quasi-inverse functor, the functor \(\mathsf{R}\Phi\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} \Phi\)).

  3. Let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\). Let \(Y\) be an object of \(\mathscr{C}\) and \(X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\) (resp. \(Y\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} X\)) a quasi-isomorphism. The object \(\mathsf{R}\Phi\circ Q(X)\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} \Phi\circ Q(X)\)) is isomorphic to \(Q\circ \Phi(Y)\).

  4. The functor \(X\mapsto \mathsf{R}\Phi\circ Q(X)\) (resp. \(X\mapsto \mathsf{L} \Phi\circ Q(X)\)) is isomorphic to the functor \(X\mapsto \varinjlim_{X/\mathsf{Qis}^\ast} Q\circ\Phi(-)\) (resp. \(X\mapsto \varinjlim_{\mathsf{Qis}^\ast/X} Q\circ \Phi(-)\)).

  5. The functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}\circ \Phi:\mathsf{K}^\ast(\mathscr{A})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) admits a cohomological derived functor on the right (resp. on the left), which is none other than the functor \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}\circ\mathsf{R}\Phi\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{H}}^0{}\circ \mathsf{L}\Phi\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.4

Suppose that \(\ast=+\) (resp. \(\ast=-\)) in the hypotheses of the preceding theorem, and that \(\mathscr{A}\) has enough injectives (resp. of projectives). Then Theorem 4.2.3 applies, taking for \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of injective (resp. projective) complexes. Suppose moreover that \(\mathscr{A}\) is of finite cohomological dimension; then the theorem applies, without restriction on \(\ast\), taking for \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of injective (resp. projective) complexes.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2.5

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) and \(\mathscr{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{B}\) an additive functor.

We shall say that \(f\) is of finite cohomological dimension on the right (resp. on the left) if \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^- f\)) exists and if there exists an integer \(m\geqslant 0\) such that for every integer \(n>m\), \(\mathsf{R}^n f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^{-n} f\)) is zero on the objects coming from \(\mathscr{A}\) via the functor \(D\). The cohomological dimension on the right (resp. on the left) of \(f\) is then the smallest of the integers \(m\) having the above property. If \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^- f\)) exists and if \(f\) is not of finite cohomological dimension, we shall say that \(f\) is of infinite cohomological dimension.

An object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\) will be said to be \(f\)-acyclic on the right (resp. on the left) if for every integer \(n>0\), \(\mathsf{R}^n f(D(X)) = 0\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^{-n} f(D(X))=0\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.6

The data are those of Definition 4.2.5. Suppose that there exists a set \(\sigma\) of objects of \(\mathscr{A}\), stable under direct sum, having the following properties:

  1. Every acyclic complex \(\in \operatorname{Ob}{\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})}\) (resp. \(\in\operatorname{Ob}{\mathsf{K}^-(\mathscr{A})}\)) of objects of \(\sigma\) is transformed by \(f\) into an acyclic complex.

  2. Every object \(X\) of \(\mathscr{A}\) injects into (resp. is a quotient of) an object of \(\sigma\). The hypotheses of Theorem 2.4.3 are satisfied by taking \(\ast=+\) (resp. \(\ast=-\)) and by taking for the category \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of complexes whose objects, in every degree, are elements of \(\sigma\). The elements of \(\sigma\) are right (resp. left) \(f\)-acyclic objects.

If moreover \(f\) is of finite cohomological dimension on the right (resp. on the left), the set of right (resp. left) \(f\)-acyclic objects [possesses, in addition to properties (1) and (2) above, property (2) of Proposition 3.1.9. Theorem 4.2.3 then applies to the functor \(\mathsf{K} f\) by taking for the category \(\mathscr{C}\) the category of complexes whose objects are right (resp. left) \(f\)-acyclic in every degree. The functor \(\mathsf{R} f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L} f\)) exists and induces on \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\) the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^+ f\)) and on \(\mathsf{D}^-(\mathscr{A})\) the functor \(\mathsf{R}^- f\) (resp. \(\mathsf{L}^- f\)).
4.3 Product. Composition

Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an abelian category and \(F:\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A}) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Ab}\) a cohomological functor. Let \(X^\bullet\) and \(Y^\bullet\) be two objects of \(\mathsf{C}(\mathscr{A})\). The functor \(F\) defines a map:
\[ \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \hom_{\mathsf{Ab}}(F(D(X^\bullet)),F(D(Y^\bullet))) \]
whence a pairing: \(F(D(X^\bullet))\times \operatorname{Ext}^0(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} F(D(Y^\bullet))\).
This pairing gives, by applying translations, pairings:
\[ F^i(D(X^\bullet))\times \operatorname{Ext}^j(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet) \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} F^{i+j}(D(Y^\bullet)) \text{.} \]

These pairings, applied to the cohomological derived functors, are none other, by definition, than the Yoneda products. The properties of these products follow immediately from this definition. We shall not develop them here.

Let \(\mathscr{A}\), \(\mathscr{A}'\), \(\mathscr{A}''\) be three abelian categories and \(f:\mathscr{A}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}'\), \(g:\mathscr{A}'\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathscr{A}''\) two additive functors. Suppose that the functors \(\mathsf{R}^+ f\) and \(\mathsf{R}^+ g\) exist. I do not know how to deduce from this that the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ g\circ f\) exists, and even if this latter functor exists, it is probably not true in general that one has the formula:
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}^+ g\circ f\ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R}^+ g \circ \mathsf{R}^+ f } \]
We have, however, the following proposition:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3.1

Suppose that the category \(\mathscr{A}'\) has enough right \(g\)-acyclic objects and that the category \(\mathscr{A}\) has enough right \(f\)-acyclic objects transformed by \(f\) into right \(g\)-acyclic objects. Then the functor \(\mathsf{R}^+ g\circ f\) exists and one has an isomorphism:

\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{R}^+ g\circ f \ar[r]^-\sim & \mathsf{R}^+ g \circ \mathsf{R}^+ f . } \]
Analogous statements for the left derived functors.

footnotes.html: A more tractable (and in practice equivalent) definition is given in [2].

blocks.html: 5 Examples
5.1 The functor \(\mathsf{Rhom}^\bullet\)
Let \(\mathscr{A}\) be an abelian category having enough injectives.

The functor \(Y\mapsto \hom^\bullet(X^\bullet,Y^\bullet)\) (1.3), where \(X^\bullet\) is an object of \(\mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A})\) and \(Y^\bullet\) an object of \(\mathsf{K}^+(\mathscr{A})\), admits a total derived functor on the right (Corollary 4.2.4), which will be denoted \(\mathsf{R}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X^\bullet,-)\). Let \(Y\) be an object of \(\mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A})\); the functor

\begin{align*} \mathsf{K}(\mathscr{A}) &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}(\mathsf{Ab}) \\ X^\bullet &\mapsto \mathsf{R}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(X^\bullet,Y) \end{align*}
is exact and vanishes on acyclic complexes, whence an exact bifunctor
\[ \xymatrix{ \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})^\circ \times \mathsf{D}^+(\mathscr{A}) \ar[r] & \mathsf{D}(\mathsf{Ab}) } \]
which we shall denote by \(\mathsf{Rhom}^\bullet\).
When \(\mathscr{A}\) is of finite cohomological dimension, the functor \(\mathsf{Rhom}^\bullet\) extends to \(\mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})^\circ\times \mathsf{D}(\mathscr{A})\) (loc. cit.).
If in addition \(\mathscr{A}\) has enough projectives, one can derive the functor \(\hom\) with respect to the first argument. The two definitions coincide in their common domain of validity.
5.2 \(\underline{\operatorname{Tor}}\) of sheaves

Let \(E\) be a ringed site (in particular a ringed topological space), \(\mathscr{A}\) the sheaf of rings, and \(\mathsf{Mod}(E)\) the category of \(\mathscr{A}\)-modules. An object \(X\) of \(\mathsf{Mod}(E)\) is said to be \(\mathscr{A}\)-flat if for every exact sequence:
\[ \xymatrix{ 0 \ar[r] & Y' \ar[r] & Y \ar[r] & Y'' \ar[r] & 0 } \]

the sequence \(0 \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y'\otimes_\mathscr{A} X \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y\otimes_\mathscr{A} X \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} Y''\otimes_\mathscr{A} X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} 0\) is exact. There exist enough \(\mathscr{A}\)-flat objects: the direct sums of objects \(\mathscr{A}_U\), where \(U\) is an object of \(E\) and \(\mathscr{A}_U\) the sheaf \(\mathscr{A}\) “extended by zero outside \(U\).” Theorem 4.2.3 therefore applies and one can define the functor

\begin{align*} \mathsf{D}^-(E,\mathscr{A}) \times \mathsf{D}^-(E,\mathscr{A}) &\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{D}^-(E,\mathscr{A}) \\ (X,Y) &\mapsto X\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} Y \end{align*}
the total tensor product, left derived functor of the tensor product functor. One thus defines, by passing to cohomology, the \(\underline{\operatorname{Tor}}_i^\mathscr{A}(X,Y)\): local hyper-tor.

The category \(\mathsf{Mod}(E)\) having enough injectives, one can derive the functor \(\hom^\bullet(X,Y)\): the complex of local homomorphisms, whence \(\mathsf{Rhom}(X,Y)\) (\(X\in \mathsf{D}\), \(Y\in \mathsf{D}^+\)).
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two objects of \(\mathsf{D}^-(E,\mathscr{A})\), and \(Z\) an object of \(\mathsf{D}^+(E,\mathscr{A})\). There exists a functorial isomorphism:
\[ \xymatrix{ \hom_{\mathsf{D}(E,\mathscr{A})}(X\overset{\mathsf{L}}{\otimes} Y,Z) \ar[r]^-\sim &\hom_{\mathsf{D}(E,\mathscr{A})}(X,\mathsf{Rhom}(Y,Z)) . } \]
5.3 Left derived functor of the inverse image
Let \(f:E\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} E'\) be a map of ringed topological spaces. The inverse image functor:
\[ f^\ast:\mathsf{Mod}(E') \mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow} \mathsf{Mod}(E) \]

is not necessarily exact. But one knows how to define \(f^\ast\)-flat objects, and there exist enough such objects. One therefore knows how to define the functor \(\mathsf{L}^- f^\ast\). One likewise has a duality formula:
Let \(X\) be an object of \(\mathsf{D}^-(E,\mathscr{A})\) and \(Y\) an object of \(\mathsf{D}^+(E',\mathscr{A}')\); there exists a functorial isomorphism:
\[ \xymatrix{ \hom_{\mathsf{D}(E',\mathscr{A}')}(\mathsf{L}^- f^\ast(X),Y) \ar[r]^-\sim & \hom_{\mathsf{D}(E,\mathscr{A})}(X,\mathsf{R}^+ f_\ast(Y)) . } \]
